header:
Date: 2025-11-03 | Start: 16:00 UTC | Duration: 62m
Redwood: Marcus Lee, Priya Nambiar, Tomás Ruiz, June Park | Nimbus Payments: Elena Park, Ravi Shah, Sofia Mendes, Chris D.
summary: 30-minute product walkthrough focused on how Redwood handles long-context sessions, high-TPS sustained load, and streaming backpressure/timeouts. Demonstration of Console metrics, Optimize recommendations, and a short synthetic failover showing graceful degradation to a lower-cost variant. Customer concerns: token billing for very long contexts, socket timeouts on mobile clients, and audit log retention for private deployments.
topics: long context handling (KV cache, prefix caching)
benchmarks and next steps for POC
transcript:
[00:00] Marcus Lee: hey everyone, thanks for joining. small agenda: long context, high throughput, streaming backpressure, then Q&A. Elena - you said you'd share some context up front?
[00:10] Elena Park: yeah, thanks. quick note, we process a lot of session history for disputes - typical session size now is like 30k tokens, but we have some edge cases up to ~150k because of multi-turn email threads. main ask: how do you keep latencies reasonable and costs predictable?
[00:25] Marcus Lee: good, that helps. Priya, do you want to kick off the long-context part?
[00:28] Priya Nambiar: sure. so Redwood has a bunch of knobs - K-V cache for previously seen prefixes, selective prefix truncation, and our runtime can pick a quantized variant for cost-sensitive workloads. quick caveat: transcriber note, K-V sometimes shown as K V in docs.
[00:45] Ravi Shah: when you say K-V cache, are we storing full token state in memory per session? got concerns about memory blowout if we keep 10k sessions at 150k tokens each.
[00:55] Priya Nambiar: yep great question. we don't keep full raw tokens for all sessions in memory. we have configurable retention windows; we materialize KV pages on GPU only for active sessions, and older prefixes are stored in cold cache on host memory or blob storage with async prefetch. the runtime pages in only what it needs for the next decode window. that said, if you pin everything you'll see linear memory growth.
[01:20] Sofia Mendes: so what are the failure modes when prefetch lags? does the caller see a big latency spike or an error?
[01:26] Tomás Ruiz: usually a latency spike; in extreme cases if the blob read fails you'll see a fallback path where we load a compatible smaller-context model or a truncated context. that's part of graceful degradation - we avoid hard errors by downgrading model variant or truncating oldest prefix.
[01:40] Chris D.: from a security perspective, where's the cold cache stored for Redwood Private? we need KMS/HSM integration and audit logs.
[01:46] June Park: for Private deployments we plug into customer KMS/HSM and write audit events to your SIEM via secure syslog/S3. the cold cache blobs live in customer-managed object store (S3/GCS on-prem adapter) when requested. we log read/write with request IDs.
[02:05] Marcus Lee: switching to high TPS. customer said peak per-region is around 4k-6k rps, sustained during peak windows. is that correct?
[02:12] Elena Park: yes, plus bursty batches for settlement runs -- maybe up to 12k for 30 minutes.
[02:18] Priya Nambiar: okay, demo time. I'm going to show the Console: per-route token throughput, per-model latency percentiles, and the autoscaler heatmap. note the auto-batching histogram and queue lengths.
[02:30] [screen share starts, minor audio glitch detected]
[02:35] Priya Nambiar: right now we have a synthetic load: 5k rps with 2k concurrent sessions, average request length 600 tokens, tail latency P99 about 210ms on Dedicated pool. watch the batching efficiency--when we get solid request shape batching reduces per-token GPU work.
[02:55] Ravi Shah: is that batching configurable by us? we have a microservice that cannot tolerate >250ms tail.
[03:00] Priya Nambiar: yes, you can set max_batch_latency and max_batch_size per model route in the Console or via API. you can also pin a route to low-latency topology with smaller batches and higher cost.
[03:12] Elena Park: what's the billing implication of batching - do we still pay per-token even if the model did internal amortization?
[03:17] Marcus Lee: billing stays per-token; batching just reduces GPU compute per token and thus cost to us which is reflected in cheaper Dedicated margins. we can present a cost model to approximate savings at different batch shapes.
[03:30] [05:00] Priya Nambiar: i'm toggling a simulated region failure to show graceful degradation. you'll see traffic shift and fallback to hosted cold pool in a different region. note: we have rate limiters and circuit breakers to avoid cascading overload.
[03:47] [small pause, typing noises]
[03:50] Priya Nambiar: ok, triggered — routing policy moved 18% of traffic to fallback variant; P99 jumped to 520ms for those requests but majority stayed under 300ms.
[04:00] Elena Park: can we control that routing policy? i.e. we want to avoid sending PII to a hosted fallback in some regs.
[04:05] Marcus Lee: absolutely - you can set data residency policies and hard pins so traffic never leaves a region. fallback then becomes smaller model variants within same region or queueing.
[04:12] Sofia Mendes: streaming backpressure - our mobile clients often hit socket closures after 30s. how does Redwood handle streaming interruptions?
[04:20] Tomás Ruiz: two paths: on the server side we support chunked streaming over HTTP and gRPC streaming with reconnect semantics. on client disconnect we keep the decoder state for a configurable grace window (default 60s) to allow reconnection. after the grace window we checkpoint and free GPU memory. if the client can't reconnect we can persist partial outputs to the session store.
[04:40] Ravi Shah: the 60s grace is fine, but can we tune it down for mobile clients to conserve memory?
[04:45] Tomás Ruiz: yes, per-route streaming_keepalive and reconnect_window are adjustable. also Optimize will recommend a different chunk size for streaming to reduce per-chunk overhead.
[04:55] [05:15] Priya Nambiar: quick demo of streaming backpressure - i'm going to artificially slow a client to 100 ms chunk ACK and then spike another client to saturate the network. watch the per-connection buffer and backpressure counters.
[05:25] [simulated spike, console graphs flicker]
[05:27] Priya Nambiar: you can see backpressure triggered; our runtime starts shedding non-critical prefetched KV pages and increases batching windows to keep throughput. Controller shows alerts and suggests switch to a lower-throughput allocation.
[05:40] Elena Park: does shedding KV pages cause hallucinations or context loss?
[05:45] Priya Nambiar: it can, which is why we surfaced a degradation score in Optimize that predicts quality drop based on the amount and recency of dropped prefixes. for critical flows we prefer to pin smaller contexts or offload cold prefixes to a cheap read-optimized store that has faster prefetch.
[06:00] Chris D.: timeouts: we have a gateway that times out at 30s - that will kill streaming. any recommendations?
[06:06] June Park: set gateway idle-timeout > expected stream duration or use a heartbeat chunk. another pattern is immediate partial response + continue in background with callback webhook when complete - that avoids long-lived sockets. we demoed a callback pattern in docs.
[06:20] Marcus Lee: ok quick diversion to cost-control features in Optimize: per-route quantization suggestions, suggested batch settings, and a predicted token-rate vs cost curve. you can run simulations with your real traces.
[06:33] Elena Park: how do we feed traces for simulation? is there an uploader or API?
[06:37] Marcus Lee: you can upload a zipped session trace through the Console or point to an S3 bucket; we ingest and run a dry-run simulator and return a suggested config.
[06:45] [07:05] Ravi Shah: we saw a 1.2x cost delta between hosted and dedicated in your benchmark; what about under 12k burst?
[07:12] Priya Nambiar: Dedicated shines for sustained throughput. for short bursts we recommend a hybrid: Dedicated base with hosted burst capacity. our routing policy will prefer Dedicated and spill to hosted only for short windows; we bill hosted usage separately.
[07:25] Sofia Mendes: for POC - what logs and traces do you need from us to reproduce the failure scenario?
[07:30] Priya Nambiar: session traces, TLS handshake logs if you can, gateway timeout settings, vectors of typical prompt lengths, and a couple of recorded failing sessions. we'll also want a service account to spin up a dedicated test pool in your VPC if doing private.
[07:45] [08:00] Demo: we run a blue/green failover where we intentionally add latency on the regional fabric to trigger a fallback. results: overall success rate dropped from 99.9% to 98.6% during the 2-minute window but graceful fallbacks prevented hard 5xxs.
[08:20] Elena Park: that's promising. any gotchas for long-context where the TTL of KV is accidental cause of degraded accuracy?
[08:26] Priya Nambiar: yes - default TTLs are tuned for average sessions; for your long threads we'll either extend TTL for pinned sessions or implement a progressive compression transform that summarizes older conversation into a condensed chunk preserving key facts. that reduces KV size and preserves performance.
[08:45] [08:55] Marcus Lee: let's talk POC mechanics briefly: we propose a 4-week POC with two phases - week 1 ingest sample traces and run dry-run; week 2-3 run live load tests with Dedicated + hosted burst; week 4 evaluate quality/regressions and iterate.
[09:10] Elena Park: timeline wise we want production gating before holiday settlement cycle in late Dec; that fits.
[09:15] Chris D.: one more on compliance - SOC2+ISO - do you provide a shared responsibility matrix?
[09:20] June Park: yes, we'll send SOC2 report redacted and a shared responsibility doc. for Private we can support offline audits.
[09:30] [09:50] Rapid Q&A and clarifications - some crosstalk, audience mics glitch. transcription note: a couple of names may be misattributed.
[10:05] Marcus Lee: recap of next steps - we'll share the recording, the benchmark sheet, and a draft SOW for the POC. Priya will own the first test run; Sofia will provide sample traces.
[10:18] Elena Park: thanks all. one ask: please include the Optimize simulation output in the SOW.
[10:22] Marcus Lee: will do. thanks everyone.
[10:25] [meeting ends]

Notes on transcription imperfections: occasional words like "prefetch" transcribed as "pre-fetch", "KV" sometimes spaced, and speaker labels may shift.
